strengths: Significance: Scheduling tool-augmented inference is a useful systems problem. The manuscript identifies concrete interactions between API return lengths, KV-cache handling, and queueing that ordinary request-length scheduling can overlook.

Originality: Combining policy-dependent memory-time costs, reprioritization after tool returns, and adaptive token budgets is a plausible contribution. Equations (9)–(25) provide a concrete formulation rather than only a conceptual proposal.

Empirical merits: Evaluation covers two datasets, three GPU configurations, Poisson and bursty arrivals, and both average and tail latency. The reported improvements over vLLM and InferCept are substantial, and Figure 10 provides initial evidence that both scheduling and batching contribute.

Presentation: The motivation, design, and evaluation are organized clearly, with explicit equations and scheduler pseudocode. The use of established datasets raises no evident material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—fairness rule: Section 4.3 prioritizes smaller scheduling costs, but Equation (26) adds alpha times waiting time. For positive alpha, waiting increases cost and therefore lowers priority, contrary to the claimed anti-starvation effect. Neither alpha's sign/value nor sorting direction is specified sufficiently to resolve this. Moreover, Algorithm 1 prioritizes running and swapped queues before new requests, so aging within queues alone does not establish fairness across queues. No waiting-time bound or request-class fairness evaluation supports the starvation-prevention claim.

Evaluation and originality: The main comparisons are against FCFS systems. There is no predicted-length SJF baseline, cost-based single-stage scheduler, or implementation of the closely related scheduling approaches cited in Section 6, including augmented-LLM scheduling work [31]. Figure 10 adds the entire two-stage scheduler at once; it does not isolate runtime correction, API-aware costs, or aging. Consequently, the experiments do not establish whether the proposed machinery improves materially over simpler scheduling changes.

Measurement validity: The normalized-latency SLO is defined as 10 times iteration time, but the reference iteration time and whether it is shared across systems are unspecified. This matters because batching changes iteration time. For 30-minute overloaded runs, the manuscript also does not explain draining, censoring, or treatment of unfinished requests; attainment is defined only over completed requests. These choices can favor schedulers that defer expensive requests. Tables 3 and 7 additionally imply approximately 1,800-second denominators across the fixed-2,000-request experiments, requiring clarification of the claimed completion-efficiency measurement.

Reproducibility: Important implementation choices are missing: software versions, baseline token budgets and tuning, alpha, beta bounds, profiled target_max values, memory reserves, and predictor training settings and length buckets. The manuscript does not adequately explain whether tool executions are live or replayed, how call durations and multi-call traces are constructed, or whether serving evaluation exclusively uses held-out predictor data. Reported results lack repeated-run uncertainty.

Soundness—resource model: The memory-time scores assume simplified token processing and swapping behavior, but their accuracy or ranking quality is not validated against measured costs. Dynamic batching counts paused memory as reclaimable by default, without specifying the reclamation policy and overhead. Its positive lower clamp can also exceed the calculated available-memory budget; the additional feasibility checks needed to ensure safety are not described. Thus the claimed stability is not established by Equations (27)–(32) alone.

Predictor evidence: Bucket accuracy of 65%/85% is difficult to interpret without bucket definitions or error distributions, and API-duration mean squared error is reported in seconds rather than squared seconds. There is no prediction-error sensitivity study or oracle comparison. Table 4 reports predictor overhead only as a percentage of potentially long request completion times, which does not establish negligible absolute overhead relative to the one-second TTFT target.

Limitations and significance: Experiments use GPT-J-6B and OPT-13B, with insufficient characterization of tool-call multiplicity, long contexts, or unseen APIs to support broad claims about contemporary agent-serving workloads. The manuscript should explicitly delimit this scope and discuss the trade-off between aggregate goodput and service for costly requests. These limitations would not independently preclude acceptance, but the unresolved correctness and evaluation issues prevent the reported gains from providing reliable support for the central claims.

strengths: Significance: Scheduling tool-augmented inference is a useful systems problem. The manuscript identifies relevant interactions among API latency, returned tokens, and KV-cache handling; Table 1 also demonstrates sensitivity to batch-token limits.

Originality: Combining policy-aware resource-cost estimates, reprioritization after tool returns, and adaptive batching is a plausible specialized contribution beyond applying output-length scheduling unchanged.

Empirical merits: Evaluation covers two datasets, two models, and three hardware configurations. Fixed-duration and fixed-request workloads, burstiness experiments, tail-latency results, and component ablations provide useful breadth. The reported improvements over vLLM and InferCept are substantial.
Presentation: The overall motivation and modular design are understandable, and the equations, notation table, and scheduler pseudocode help expose the proposed mechanism.
weaknesses: Soundness—comparisons do not establish the central scheduling contribution. The main baselines use FCFS; there is no comparison with predicted shortest-job-first, processing-time ranking, or the cited learned schedulers under equivalent cache handling and batching. Section 6 states that AugServe also integrates chunked prefill, but equivalent baseline configuration is not established. Figure 10 does not isolate Stage II, API-aware scoring, or aging, so the gains cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed two-stage design.

Soundness—the anti-starvation rule is inconsistent as specified. Section 4.3 prioritizes lower costs, but Equation 26 adds α times waiting time. For positive α, this reduces the priority of older requests. Neither the sign/value of α nor the sorting direction resolves this ambiguity. Algorithm 1 additionally gives running and swapped queues precedence over waiting queues, without explaining how aging prevents starvation across queues. No waiting-time-by-request-length or starvation experiment supports the fairness claim.

Soundness—the cost and batching models lack validation. Equations 9–25 use memory-time estimates and simplified iteration costs without showing that their rankings predict actual resource pressure or completion times. Proposition 1 is valid within its simplified model but omits tool waiting and cache-handling overhead. Equations 31–32 count paused memory as reclaimable, while the subsequent lower bound can exceed the calculated available budget; reclamation, feasibility checks, and stability under this condition are insufficiently specified.

Evaluation validity: The 30-minute experiments do not explain how unfinished requests, queue draining, and warm-up are handled. SLO attainment is explicitly calculated over completed requests, which can obscure requests left waiting by a cost-prioritizing scheduler. The fixed-request results are helpful, but the iteration-time reference used to set the normalized-latency SLO is unspecified. These details matter for interpreting the large goodput ratios under overload.

Reproducibility: The manuscript omits important implementation and configuration details, including software versions, baseline token limits, α, β bounds, profiling procedure for target_max, predictor bucket boundaries, and training hyperparameters. It also does not clearly describe API execution versus trace replay or establish that serving evaluation excludes predictor-training examples. No code artifact, repeated-run variability, or confidence intervals are provided. Table 4 reports prediction overhead only as a fraction of potentially long request latency, which does not establish negligible absolute overhead.

Limitations and ethics: Generality is tested only with GPT-J-6B and OPT-13B, without characterizing longer contexts, tool-call counts, or prediction distribution shift. The manuscript does not adequately discuss these limits or the service-allocation consequences of favoring inexpensive requests. No material research-ethics violation is evident, but fairness and stability claims exceed the evidence. Overall, the useful problem and promising measurements do not overcome the unresolved methodological and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Tool-augmented inference is an important serving workload. The manuscript identifies useful scheduling signals beyond total sequence length, including API return length, call duration, and KV-cache handling policy. Figures 5–6 and Table 2 motivate accounting for these differences.

Originality: Combining predictive admission priorities, reprioritization after tool returns, and memory-adaptive batching is a plausible systems contribution. Updating priorities using observed API returns is particularly relevant to multiround requests.

Empirical merits: The evaluation covers two datasets, two models, three hardware configurations, and both Poisson and bursty arrivals. The reported improvements over vLLM and InferCept are substantial, and the fixed-request experiments, tail-latency measurements, and component ablation provide useful additional evidence.
Presentation: The motivation and overall architecture are understandable, with explicit cost equations, scheduler pseudocode, and supplementary results.
weaknesses: Soundness and attribution: The main comparisons are against FCFS systems, so they do not establish the benefit of the proposed scheduling rule over simpler alternatives. There is no matched predicted-length/SJF baseline, despite discussing length-aware schedulers and citing directly relevant augmented-inference work [31]. Figure 10 adds batching and then the complete scheduler, but does not isolate runtime correction, API-aware costs, or prediction accuracy. Comparisons against these alternatives and a well-tuned static token limit are needed to substantiate the central contribution.

Fairness is unsupported and the stated rule is ambiguous. Section 4.3 prioritizes lower scheduling costs, but Equation 26 adds alpha times waiting time. For positive alpha, this lowers the priority of older requests, contrary to the anti-starvation claim; neither alpha's sign nor its value is specified. Algorithm 1 also gives running and swapped queues precedence over new requests, without explaining how aging overcomes this hierarchy. Aggregate P95 latency does not establish starvation prevention, especially when measurements exclude unfinished requests.

Evaluation accounting needs clarification. W1/W3 stop after 30 minutes, and SLO attainment is defined over completed requests; treatment of unfinished requests and queue draining is unspecified. This matters when comparing FCFS with a scheduler favoring inexpensive requests under overload. Moreover, Tables 3 and 7 imply approximately 1,800-second denominators throughout the supposedly fixed-request completion-efficiency experiment: for example, 2,000 requests at 100% attainment and 1.11 requests/s imply about 1,802 seconds. The actual completion times and denominator conventions must be reported. The normalized-latency SLO also needs an explicit, common iteration-time reference across systems.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the reported gains. The manuscript omits software versions, baseline token budgets and feature settings, alpha and beta values, profiling details, predictor bucket boundaries and training hyperparameters, and run-to-run uncertainty. It is unclear whether serving benchmarks use only held-out predictor data and whether tool calls are executed or replayed. Section 6 states that AugServe includes chunked prefill, but equivalent baseline configuration is not established.

The resource model is insufficiently validated. Equations 9–25 rank requests using a memory-time cost proxy without demonstrating that it predicts the relevant scheduling costs or SLO outcomes. Dynamic batching counts reclaimable paused memory as available, then imposes a minimum token budget that can exceed the calculated capacity; the eviction procedure and final memory-feasibility safeguards are not specified. These gaps prevent assessing the claimed stability.

Scope and limitations: Experiments use GPT-J-6B and OPT-13B, without establishing transfer to contemporary tool-capable models or realistic multiround execution. Predictor robustness is not tested despite only 65% output-length classification accuracy on Merge. No material research-ethics violation is apparent, but the manuscript should explicitly discuss workload representativeness, prediction failures, and service fairness. Overall, the promising idea and large reported gains do not yet overcome the evidential and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Scheduling tool-augmented LLM requests is an important systems problem. The manuscript identifies concrete sources of inefficiency: heterogeneous resumption costs, memory occupied during external calls, and unsuitable fixed token budgets.

Originality: Combining segment-level memory–time costs, feedback at tool returns, and adaptive batch budgets is a useful extension of length-based scheduling and INFERCEPT’s context-management policies. The contribution is primarily this integration and state-dependent refinement.

Empirical merits: Evaluation spans two datasets, several model/GPU configurations, bursty arrivals, mixed workloads, and a 70B model. Comparisons include length-based SSJF and a reimplemented MARS scheduler. Table 2 provides evidence that scheduling and budget adaptation contribute complementary improvements.

Presentation: The lifecycle and architecture diagrams clearly explain the system. Appendix E appropriately acknowledges that its simplified analysis does not establish guarantees for the full online problem. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described application.
weaknesses: Soundness: The optimization formulation, priority rule, and implementation are not aligned. Equation 3 constrains instantaneous memory, whereas Equation 4 divides value by an integrated memory–time cost; this is not the corresponding knapsack value density. Algorithm 1 instead packs iteration tokens. Moreover, Appendix E’s approximation theorem requires comparing greedy packing against the best feasible singleton, which Algorithm 1 does not do. The theorem is valid for its stated simplified algorithm but does not justify the implemented packing procedure. The method should be characterized as a heuristic unless these gaps are resolved.

Evaluation validity: The large goodput gains depend on incompletely specified SLO and measurement procedures. The paper does not specify the reference single-iteration time, handling of external-call time in normalized latency, or whether TTFT is measured once per request or after resumptions. With 30-minute arrival windows and baseline delays reaching hundreds of seconds, treatment of unfinished requests, draining, and the goodput denominator is essential but absent. Figure 9 also reports substantially different average external-call times across schedulers (28 seconds for vLLM versus 76 for AugServe), requiring an explanation of workload equivalence or completion-based selection effects.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness: Missing details include software versions, baseline token budgets and tuning, Tmax and clipping bounds, predictor training/test splits and training settings, and how tool calls are executed or replayed. There is no artifact link or repeated-run uncertainty reporting. Because fixed-budget selection is itself a central motivation, comparison against appropriately tuned fixed budgets is particularly important. Appendix D.6 supplies a useful MARS comparison, but insufficient implementation detail establishes fidelity to that baseline.

Mechanistic evidence: Table 2 separates scheduling from budget adaptation but does not isolate the claimed distinctive benefit of cross-round feedback from the memory–time ranking and aging terms. Prediction robustness is tested only using symmetric multiplicative noise, without testing systematic bias or distribution shift. The assertion that a 10–20-second TTFT increase is mild is also difficult to reconcile with the stated one-second TTFT SLO.

Implementation clarity: Equation 11 does not adequately explain how free and reclaimable KV memory translate into a forward-pass token budget while accounting for resident contexts and restoration costs. Algorithm 1 stops at the first request that does not fit, rather than considering later candidates, and does not clearly refresh all waiting requests’ aging priorities each iteration. These omissions affect utilization and the claimed protection against starvation.

Limitations and practical significance: Overhead is judged against heavily queued end-to-end latency: the predictor takes approximately 180 ms per request, and scheduling takes 18–22 ms per iteration in Table 3. Their impact under lightly loaded, latency-sensitive operation is not established. Together with the measurement and reproducibility gaps, this prevents the promising reported improvements from supporting acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Significance: Scheduling tool-augmented LLM requests is an important systems problem. The manuscript identifies relevant interactions among paused requests, KV-cache management, context growth, and resumption costs.

Originality: Combining segment-dependent memory–time costs, refinement after tool returns, and adaptive batch budgets is a useful systems contribution. Its novelty lies primarily in integrating these mechanisms rather than introducing a new scheduling primitive.

Empirical merits: Evaluation spans two datasets, multiple model/GPU configurations, mixed workloads, and bursty arrivals. The appendix includes a relevant MARS comparison, tail latencies, and SLO attainment. Table 2 provides evidence that scheduling and budget adaptation contribute complementary improvements.

Presentation: The lifecycle and architecture diagrams make the main design understandable. Appendix E appropriately acknowledges that its simplified analysis does not establish guarantees for the full online problem. I found no material research-ethics concern in the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness: The optimization formulation, implemented heuristic, and approximation theorem do not match. Equation 3 constrains instantaneous memory, whereas Equation 4 ranks by value divided by integrated memory–time cost; this is not the value density of the stated knapsack problem. Appendix E proves a standard guarantee for greedy packing combined with the best feasible singleton, but Algorithm 1 has no singleton comparison and stops at the first non-fitting request rather than continuing to scan. Even within the explicitly simplified setting, the theorem therefore does not establish a guarantee for the presented scheduler. A heuristic is acceptable, but the claimed optimization interpretation needs correction.

Reproducibility: Essential implementation and experimental details are missing. The paper does not specify serving-engine versions, baseline token budgets and tuning procedures, the values of Tmax and its clipping factors, or operational formulas/profiling procedures for the component costs in Equations 7–10. Predictor training sizes, splits, hyperparameters, and inference hardware are also unspecified. The workload description does not establish whether tool calls and model outputs are replayed, simulated, or executed live. These omissions prevent reliable reconstruction of the reported gains.

Experimental attribution: The main comparison jointly changes scheduling and batch capacity, while the component ablation uses only one configuration. It does not isolate runtime refinement from the initial cost model, or reclaimable-memory accounting from ordinary budget adaptation. The MARS comparison is welcome, but uses a reimplementation without enough detail to assess fidelity. Comparisons with tuned fixed budgets and a free-memory-only adaptive budget are particularly important because these are central distinctions claimed by the paper.

Goodput evidence needs stronger controls: The largest improvements occur where baseline queues grow to hundreds of seconds and baseline goodput approaches zero. Under this overload regime, the unspecified treatment of requests remaining after the 30-minute arrival window, the measurement denominator, and queue draining can materially affect results. Only one SLO prescription is evaluated, without a clear calibration procedure for 'single-iteration time'; repeated-run uncertainty is not reported. The plots support promising relative improvements, but do not adequately establish the robustness of the headline multipliers.

Memory feasibility is underspecified: Equation 11 converts free and reclaimable memory into a per-iteration token budget, but processing tokens and resident KV-cache tokens are different quantities. Algorithm 1 does not explain how existing contexts, swap-ins, recomputation, or actual reclamation enter its tokens(r) test. Clipping the budget upward to a fixed minimum can also exceed the memory-derived value unless a separate allocator check intervenes. These details are necessary to substantiate the claimed relationship between dynamic budgeting and memory constraints.

Limitations and presentation: Several interpretations overstate the evidence. Section 6.3 calls a 10–20-second TTFT increase mild despite the stated 1-second TTFT SLO. Scheduling overhead of 18–22 ms per iteration is called negligible without comparison to forward-iteration duration. Figure 9 reports substantially different external-call latency components across systems without explaining why. The abstract's 6.5×/4.7× goodput gains also differ from Section 6.1's 7.5×/5.7× without clearly identifying the respective aggregation sets. These issues require clarification alongside a fuller discussion of overload behavior and deployment limits.

strengths: Significance: Scheduling tool-augmented LLM requests is a useful systems problem. The manuscript clearly identifies how tool latency, returned context, and KV-cache handling create heterogeneous resumption costs that length-only scheduling can miss.

Originality: The main contribution is a coherent integration of segment-level memory-time costs, priority refinement after tool returns, and a token budget that incorporates reclaimable memory. This is a plausible extension beyond the inherited INFERCEPT context-handling policies.

Empirical merits: The evaluation covers two datasets, multiple model/GPU configurations, bursty arrivals, mixed workloads, and prediction perturbations. Table 2 provides useful component ablations: scheduling increases goodput from 0.15 to 0.93 requests/s, and adding dynamic budgeting raises it to 1.07 requests/s.

Presentation: The lifecycle and architecture diagrams make the design understandable. Appendix E appropriately acknowledges that its simplified guarantee does not extend to the full online scheduling problem. I found no material research-ethics concern in the described application.
weaknesses: Soundness—objective and algorithm are not aligned. Equation 3 constrains instantaneous memory, but Equation 4 ranks by value divided by segment-integrated memory-time cost. This is not the density rule for the stated knapsack problem. Moreover, the value 1 + βw measures neither request completion nor deadline satisfaction, so its connection to goodput remains heuristic. Appendix E proves a standard result for an algorithm using matching costs and a best-singleton fallback; Algorithm 1 has no such fallback and stops at the first request that does not fit. The theorem therefore does not establish a guarantee for the presented scheduler, even before considering online dynamics.

Reproducibility is inadequate for validating the central performance claims. The manuscript does not specify engine versions, baseline token budgets and tuning, chunked-prefill/prefix-cache settings, numerical precision, predictor training sizes and held-out splits, or the values of Tmax and the budget clipping bounds. The individual memory-time cost components are not operationally specified sufficiently to reproduce their estimates. No code artifact is identified, and repeated-run variability is not reported.

Workload execution and measurement accounting need clarification. It is unclear whether tool calls and generated sequences are executed live or replayed, how identical requests and tool durations are maintained across systems, and how unfinished requests and queue draining are handled after the 30-minute arrival window. Figure 9 reports average external-call time ranging from 28 seconds for vLLM to 76 seconds for AugServe, although scheduling alone should not change fixed per-request tool durations. This could reflect different completion populations or another measurement choice, but the manuscript does not explain it. These details are essential when comparing severely overloaded systems.

Baseline comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the claimed advance. The closest method, MARS, is reimplemented and evaluated only on one model/hardware configuration with INFERCEPT-derived workloads. Its implementation fidelity is not demonstrated, and the comparison does not clearly hold token budgeting and context handling constant while changing only the scheduling rule. Similarly, Table 1 establishes that static-budget tuning strongly affects goodput, but the evaluation does not document how baseline budgets were selected.

The memory-to-token-budget mechanism is underspecified. Equation 11 converts free and reclaimable memory into tokens processed in an iteration, although processing-token count and resident KV-cache footprint differ across prefill, decode, and restoration. Algorithm 1 does not show separate memory-feasibility enforcement, swap/reclamation timing, or protection when the clipping lower bound exceeds available capacity. These omissions prevent assessing whether the proposed budget reliably enforces the stated constraint.

Limitations and claim calibration need improvement. Large relative gains primarily characterize heavily overloaded baselines under one SLO configuration; sustainable capacity at a target attainment level and sensitivity to SLO thresholds are not established. Long-request fairness also remains unresolved: Table 5 reports AugServe P99 TTFT around 99–157 seconds at its default setting despite a 1-second TTFT SLO. Predictor robustness is tested with symmetric multiplicative noise, which does not establish robustness to systematic errors or unseen tools. The useful empirical promise does not yet outweigh these evidential and reproducibility gaps.
